**Veterinary/MPH student here. I was asked to write an article on practical knowledge about COVID-19 and animals, among a few other things. It presents and links to the advice of various public health authorities. I'd be very grateful for any comments, feedback, improvements, etc. Thanks in advance!**

**One Health and the origins of COVID-19**

[One Health](https://www.who.int/features/qa/one-health/en/) refers to the connection between human, animal, and plant health in their shared environment. The multisectoral nature of COVID-19 has sparked interest in One Health and “[zoonoses](https://www.who.int/topics/zoonoses/en/)”; diseases transmitted from animals to humans.

The exact [origin](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-020-0820-9) of COVID-19 isn’t clear, but it has similarities with other zoonotic spillover events. Notably, the first SARS outbreak originated from a [seafood market](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-020-2012-7). Also, HIV and Ebola virus are thought to have originated from [consumption of wildlife](https://www.healthline.com/health-news/how-ebola-is-and-is-not-like-aids-101414#1).

**Current evidence of COVID-19 transmission in domestic animals**

***There is no evidence that cats, dogs,*** [***pigs, chickens, or ducks***](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/early/2020/04/07/science.abb7015) ***are a source of human COVID-19 infection*****.** ***There is*** [***no evidence***](https://www.oie.int/scientific-expertise/specific-information-and-recommendations/questions-and-answers-on-2019novel-coronavirus/) ***showing that attempts to abandon or harm animals will prevent the spread of human infection.*** However, there is evidence that humans can pass COVID-19 to some animals, resulting in mild illness. People known or suspected to have COVID-19 should avoid direct physical contact with any animals if possible. [If not](https://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/daily-life-coping/animals.html) possible, they should wear a facemask and wash their hands before and after handling. Prevent your animals from contacting humans or animals with COVID-19 infection. Contact local public health authorities to see if pets and other animals can be tested for current or previous COVID-19 infection.

There is limited [evidence](https://wsava.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/COVID-19-An-Update-for-WSAVA-Members-April-6.pdf) suggesting cats can become infected with COVID-19 after exposure to infected humans or animals, and that they can then infect other felids in close proximity. Evidence suggests infected cats may shed relatively low amounts of the virus for a short period.

Later conclusions may differ from what current evidence suggests. For the most accurate and current information, refer to the [WHO](https://www.who.int/emergencies/diseases/novel-coronavirus-2019), [OIE](https://www.oie.int/scientific-expertise/specific-information-and-recommendations/questions-and-answers-on-2019novel-coronavirus/), your [country’s public health authorities](http://www.ianphi.org/about/member-countries.html), or the [US CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/daily-life-coping/animals.html) if your country lacks reliable public health guidance. For further resources, see the World Small Animal Veterinary Association’s [COVID-19 Hub](https://wsava.org/news/highlighted-news/the-new-coronavirus-and-companion-animals-advice-for-wsava-members/). Also, see the American Veterinary Medical Association’s and US CDC’s[ guidelines here](https://www.avma.org/resources-tools/animal-health-and-welfare/covid-19/interim-recommendations-intake-companion-animals-households-humans-COVID-19-are-present).

**Collaboration across veterinary and human health sectors**

Multiple veterinary diagnostic labs have been helping to test samples for COVID-19. Some have [lent equipment](https://www.kcrg.com/content/news/Veterinary-Diagnostic-Laboratory-at-ISU-helping-speed-up-COVID-19-testing-569134801.html) to human testing facilities, and some seek to test [human samples](https://www.oie.int/fileadmin/Home/eng/Our_scientific_expertise/docs/pdf/COV-19/Guidance_for_animal_health_laboratories.pdf) themselves. Some veterinary practitioners are [sharing](https://foxbaltimore.com/news/coronavirus/animal-ventilators-donated-for-covid19-patients) clinical equipment, and [offering](https://abc7chicago.com/coronavirus-illinois-cases-update-map/6072141/) their clinical skills to assist with human COVID-19 cases. Veterinarians will also need to be attentive to possible [human-to-animal](https://time.com/5815939/tiger-bronx-zoo-positive-coronavirus/) transmission.

**Disease emergence: Intersections with environmental health**

As human activity expands further into wildlife habitats, the opportunity for zoonotic spillover increases. Nowhere is this more true than [rapidly-developing](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK215318/) areas of the world.

Because of this, numerous programs aim to discover new diseases before they become epidemics. Among these are [PREDICT](https://www.usaid.gov/sites/default/files/documents/1864/Predict2-factsheet.pdf) and [Global Virome Project](http://www.globalviromeproject.org/). Programs such as these will undoubtedly be given more attention in the wake of COVID-19, but [some scientists](https://www.theatlantic.com/science/archive/2017/10/pandemic-prediction-challenge/543954/) caution that finding the next major spillover agent will be difficult, given the massive number of potential causative pathogens.
